options.why: The distributed form defeats the naive single-IP response precisely because there is no single source address to block, which is why the guide names scrubbing and rate limiting instead.

options.text: Restoring from backup, since a DDoS always corrupts the underlying data alongside exhausting capacity, when confidentiality and integrity may remain entirely intact throughout a pure resource-exhaustion attack that alters nothing.
options.why: A denial of service is not a data breach; confidentiality and integrity may be entirely intact, so a restore from backup is not the relevant response to a pure availability attack.

options.text: Patching the service, since the flood must be exploiting a specific software vulnerability.
options.why: Volumetric and amplification-based denial of service exhausts resources through traffic volume, not through exploiting a named defect that patching would fix.

options.text: Enabling full disk encryption, since encrypted storage resists resource exhaustion attacks.
options.why: Disk encryption protects data confidentiality at rest and has no bearing on a network capacity or connection exhaustion attack.

items.rationale: Blocking the source IP is a valid response to a single-source denial of service, but a distributed attack has no single address whose removal stops it — upstream scrubbing, rate limiting, and added capacity are the distributed answers. Confidentiality and integrity may remain entirely intact throughout, so a data-recovery response does not apply.

items.stem: A denial-of-service attack and a ransomware attack are compared as a pair. Which axis actually separates the two, according to the guide's comparison?

options.text: Whether anything runs on the victim host — a denial of service overwhelms from outside without executing there, while malware requires code on the host by definition.
options.why: The comparison names execution on the victim as the separating axis: a DoS needs only traffic, while ransomware and malware generally require something to run.

options.text: Severity — denial of service is always classified as more severe than ransomware because it affects availability directly.
options.why: The comparison does not rank the two by severity; it separates them by whether code executes on the victim, and ransomware also affects availability once files are encrypted.

options.text: Duration — a denial of service always lasts longer than a ransomware incident.
options.why: Duration is not the property the table tracks; both can last from minutes to weeks depending on the response, and the axis is about what runs where, not how long it takes.

options.text: Attribution — denial-of-service attackers are always anonymous, while ransomware attackers always identify themselves for payment, a pattern that varies case by case for both attack types and is not the property the comparison table is built around.
options.why: Attacker identification practices vary case by case for both attack types and are not the axis the comparison table is built around.

items.rationale: The comparison's separating axis is whether anything runs on the victim host: a denial of service overwhelms a system from outside without executing on it, while malware and ransomware require code on the host and therefore leave the data itself in question in a way pure traffic exhaustion does not.

items.stem: A user on a hostile wireless access point clicks through a certificate warning rather than cancelling the connection. What does that click actually let an on-path attacker do?

options.text: Present its own certificate as if it were the real server, relay traffic in both directions, and read everything in between.
options.why: Clicking through the warning is exactly the failure mode the guide names: it defeats the certificate validation that would otherwise have exposed the attacker's inability to present a trusted certificate for the real name.

options.text: Nothing further, since TLS encryption remains effective regardless of whether the certificate warning was heeded, when clicking through the warning is exactly what lets the attacker present its own certificate as if it were the real server.
options.why: Certificate validation is what defeats a man-in-the-middle; skipping it or clicking through is one of the named ways the attack actually succeeds, not a detail encryption alone covers.

options.text: Exhaust the connection's available bandwidth, denying the user service entirely.
options.why: Resource exhaustion describes a denial-of-service attack; an on-path attacker here is relaying and reading traffic, not overwhelming capacity.

options.text: Install a rootkit on the user's device without any further action required.
options.why: A rootkit requires code execution on the victim device, which is a separate malware concern from intercepting and relaying network traffic.

items.rationale: An on-path attacker relays traffic between two parties who each believe they are talking directly to the other. Certificate validation is what defeats this, because the attacker cannot present a certificate for the real name that chains to a trusted anchor — which is exactly why clicking through the warning removes that defence.

items.stem: Which of the following gets an attacker into position for a man-in-the-middle attack in the first place, before certificate validation ever comes into play?

options.text: ARP or DNS manipulation that redirects the victim's traffic through the attacker's machine.
options.why: The guide names ARP or DNS manipulation, a hostile access point, or a compromised router as the ways an attacker gets onto the path in the first place, before validation is even tested.

options.text: A stolen but still-valid password used to log into the target service directly.
options.why: Logging in with a stolen credential is a direct authentication compromise, not positioning on the network path between two parties who believe they are talking to each other.

options.text: A phishing email that persuades the victim to click a malicious attachment.
options.why: Phishing manipulates the victim directly into an action; it does not itself place the attacker on the network path between two communicating parties.

options.text: A misconfigured `sudo` rule that lets an unprivileged local user run arbitrary commands, which grants elevated access on a host already compromised rather than positioning an attacker on the path between two remote parties.
options.why: A `sudo` misconfiguration is a local privilege-escalation route, unrelated to intercepting traffic between two remote parties.

items.rationale: Before certificate validation can even be tested, the attacker first has to get into the traffic path — through a hostile or spoofed wireless access point, ARP or DNS manipulation, or a compromised router. Validation is then what defeats the attempt, unless it is skipped or the warning is clicked through.

items.stem: A team enables account lockout after five failed logins to defend against credential stuffing. Logs later show the attack made only one or two attempts per account across thousands of different accounts. Why did lockout fail, and what would actually stop this?

options.text: Lockout never approached its threshold because stuffing makes few attempts per account; MFA is the defence that covers stuffing because a correct password stops being sufficient.
options.why: Credential stuffing replays pairs already known to be valid elsewhere, staying well under any per-account threshold, which is exactly why MFA — not lockout — is the control that generalises across all three related attacks.

options.text: Lockout worked correctly here, and the low per-account attempt count only proves the attack was unsuccessful, when stuffing makes about one or two attempts per account and lockout also opens a denial-of-service vector against real users.
options.why: The guide states lockout is the reflexive but wrong answer for stuffing and spraying specifically because those attacks stay under any lockout threshold by design.

options.text: Lockout failed because the passwords involved were too weak, and a stronger complexity policy is the actual fix.
options.why: Strong password policies do nothing against credential stuffing when the reused password was already strong; checking candidates against known-breached lists is what addresses reuse.

options.text: Lockout failed because this was actually phishing, and user awareness training is the fix instead.
options.why: Credential stuffing replays credentials the attacker already possesses and requires no action from the victim, unlike phishing, which needs the user to hand over a credential.

items.rationale: Credential stuffing tests username-password pairs already known to be valid from another breach, making roughly one or two attempts per account, so it never approaches a lockout threshold and also creates a denial-of-service vector against real users if lockout is relied on. MFA is the defence that covers brute force, stuffing, and spraying alike, because it removes the sufficiency of a correct password alone.

items.stem: Brute force and credential stuffing are compared against phishing as a pair. Which axis does the guide use to separate them?

options.text: Who supplies the credential — the attacker derives or replays it themselves in one case, and the account holder hands it over in the other.
options.why: The comparison's separating axis is exactly this: the user is unaware in a guessing or stuffing attack but has to actively participate in a phishing attack.

options.text: Which one targets a database versus which one targets an operating system.
options.why: Neither attack is defined by which layer of a system it targets; both can be aimed at any login surface regardless of what sits behind it.

options.text: Which one is automated versus which one is always performed manually by a person.
options.why: Both brute force and stuffing are automated at scale, and phishing campaigns are frequently automated too; automation level is not the table's separating property.

options.text: Which one is stopped by rate limiting versus which one is stopped only by patching software, when neither attack is defeated by patching software at all — MFA, rate limiting, breached-password checks and training are the named defences.
options.why: Neither attack is defeated by patching software; the guide names MFA, rate limiting and breached-password checks for one side and user awareness for the other.

items.rationale: The separating axis is who supplies the credential: an attacker guesses or replays it themselves in brute force and credential stuffing, with the victim unaware throughout, while phishing requires the victim to actively hand the credential over. That difference is why one is fought with rate limits and breached-password checks and the other with training.

items.stem: OWASP separates brute force, credential stuffing, and password spraying as three distinct attacks. What actually differs between password spraying and the other two?

options.text: Spraying tests one weak password against many different accounts, rather than many passwords against one account or replaying known-valid pairs.
options.why: The guide defines spraying by that inverted spread — one guess across many accounts — which is precisely what makes it hide inside normal login traffic as effectively as stuffing does.

options.text: Spraying is the only one of the three that does not require any guessing at all.
options.why: Spraying and brute force both guess; only credential stuffing replays credentials already known to be valid rather than guessing.

options.text: Spraying is the only one of the three that targets a single account exhaustively, when exhaustively targeting one account is what defines brute force, while spraying deliberately spreads a single guess across many accounts instead.
options.why: Exhaustively targeting a single account describes brute force; spraying deliberately spreads a single guess across many accounts instead.

options.text: Spraying is the only one of the three defeated by a strong password policy alone.
options.why: MFA is named as the defence covering all three attacks; a strong password policy alone does not reliably stop any of them, spraying included.

items.rationale: OWASP's three related credential attacks differ in how attempts are spread: brute force tests many passwords against one account, credential stuffing replays known-valid pairs from another breach, and password spraying tests one weak password against a large number of different accounts, which is what lets it hide inside normal login traffic.

items.stem: A web application builds a SQL statement by concatenating a search term straight from the request into the query string. What is the single design error underlying SQL injection and cross-site scripting alike?

options.text: Concatenating untrusted input into a string that something else will parse, so attacker-controlled text changes the statement's meaning.
options.why: The guide names this one root cause across databases, shells, LDAP and HTML output, which is why the same class of fix generalises to all of them.

options.text: Storing user data without hashing it before it reaches the database.
options.why: Hashing concerns how a value is stored, not whether untrusted input is allowed to alter a statement's structure, which is the actual mechanism behind injection.

options.text: Running the database service with more privilege than its task requires, which worsens the impact of a successful injection rather than being the design error that makes the injection possible in the first place.
options.why: Over-privileged service accounts worsen the impact of a successful injection but are not the design error that makes injection possible in the first place.

options.text: Failing to encrypt the connection between the application and the database.
options.why: Transport encryption protects the connection from interception; it has no bearing on whether untrusted input is allowed to change a query's structure.

items.rationale: SQL injection and cross-site scripting share one design error: untrusted input is concatenated into a string that a database, shell, or browser then parses as structure rather than as data. The fix generalises across all of them because the root cause is the same regardless of which interpreter is targeted.

items.stem: A developer proposes fixing an injection vulnerability by escaping special characters in the user input before concatenating it into the query. What does OWASP name as the fix that should come first instead?

options.text: A safe API that never builds the statement by concatenation at all, such as a parameterised query or prepared statement.
options.why: OWASP puts a safe API first because it keeps data and query structure in separate channels, so input cannot change the statement's meaning regardless of what characters it contains.

options.text: Escaping is already the primary defence, and parameterised queries are only a supporting measure.
options.why: The guide reverses this: escaping and server-side validation are supporting measures, while a safe API that avoids concatenation entirely is the primary defence.

options.text: Enabling mandatory access control on the database process, which prevents any injected query from executing, when mandatory access control confines what a compromised process can reach on the filesystem rather than stopping a malformed query from parsing.
options.why: Mandatory access control confines what a compromised process can reach on the filesystem; it does not prevent a malformed query from being parsed and executed in the first place.

options.text: Rate limiting requests to the endpoint that accepts the search term.
options.why: Rate limiting slows the volume of requests but does not stop a single malicious request from injecting a payload into the query.

items.rationale: OWASP's primary defence is a safe API — parameterised queries, prepared statements, or an ORM — that keeps data and query structure in separate channels so input cannot change the statement's meaning. Positive server-side validation and context-appropriate escaping support that primary defence rather than replacing it.

items.stem: An attacker who phished a low-privilege credential then exploits a writable service unit to obtain a root shell on the same host. Is the exploit itself the way the attacker got in?

options.text: No — it is a post-access step; the phished credential was the way in, and the writable service unit is what turned that limited access into more.
options.why: The guide is explicit that escalation is a post-access step, not a way in, and that ordering is exactly what the exam tests.

options.text: Yes, since gaining root through the writable unit is itself the moment initial access occurred.
options.why: Initial access already happened through the phished credential; the writable unit is what let the attacker reach beyond what that access already allowed.

options.text: This describes horizontal escalation, since the attacker moved to a peer account rather than upward, when moving from a low-privilege account up to root is the vertical case, not a sideways move to a peer account at the same level.
options.why: Moving from a low-privilege account to root is vertical escalation, moving up in privilege, not horizontal movement to a peer account at the same level.

options.text: This is denial of service, since the writable service unit was used to disrupt the host.
options.why: Nothing here disrupts availability; the attacker instead gains more access than they started with, which is what escalation names.

items.rationale: Privilege escalation turns access already obtained into more access than was granted; it is a post-access step, not a way in. An attacker who phished a credential still needed that credential to gain initial access — the writable service unit is what let them reach further from that foothold.

items.stem: An ordinary user discovers a SUID binary that can be made to run arbitrary commands, and uses it to reach another ordinary user's private files rather than root. Which kind of privilege escalation is this?

options.text: Horizontal escalation — reaching another account's data at the same privilege level rather than moving up to root.
options.why: The guide defines horizontal escalation as moving sideways to another account at the same level, which is exactly what reading a peer's private files without gaining root describes.

options.text: Vertical escalation, since any SUID exploitation always ends in a root shell by definition.
options.why: Vertical escalation specifically means moving up to root or administrator; a SUID exploit that only reaches a peer account's data at the same level is not vertical.

options.text: Not privilege escalation at all, since no new privileges beyond the original account were technically granted and the account only used access it already held.
options.why: Reaching data outside the scope the original account was authorised for is the definition of escalation, whether the movement is sideways or upward.

options.text: An insider threat, since the attacker already had a legitimate account on the system.
options.why: Insider threat concerns harm from someone whose own legitimate access is misused, not a technique for reaching a different account's data entirely.

items.rationale: Vertical escalation moves up in privilege, typically to root or administrator; horizontal escalation moves sideways, reaching another account's data or access at the same privilege level. Using a SUID binary to read a peer's private files without ever gaining root is the horizontal case.

items.stem: A contractor with legitimate database access exports records for personal gain. Why do MFA, perimeter filtering, and patching all fail to engage against this specific actor?

options.text: The contractor already authenticated legitimately and never crosses the perimeter or exploits a software flaw, so none of those controls has a reason to trigger.
options.why: The guide states plainly that the insider passes authentication legitimately, which is exactly why the controls that dominate the rest of this competency do not engage at all.

options.text: Those controls only ever apply to attacks originating from outside the country the organisation operates in.
options.why: Geography plays no role in why these controls miss an insider; the reason is that the actor's access is legitimate, not where they are located.

options.text: MFA, perimeter filtering, and patching are all detective controls, and only preventive controls can address an insider, when MFA, perimeter filtering and patching are all preventive controls to begin with, and what actually addresses an insider is a different set entirely.
options.why: MFA, filtering and patching are preventive controls; what actually addresses an insider is a different set of preventive and detective controls, not a shift in control type generally.

options.text: The controls do engage, but only after the contractor's session has already ended for the day.
options.why: There is no delayed engagement here; these controls simply have nothing to check, since the contractor's login and access were already legitimate throughout.

items.rationale: An insider already holds legitimate access, so they pass authentication normally, never cross a perimeter to be filtered, and exploit no software flaw for patching to address. What does apply is least privilege and need-to-know limiting reach, separation of duties, and accounting and auditing to detect and attribute the misuse afterward.

items.stem: An employee accidentally makes a customer storage bucket public rather than deliberately leaking it. Does the guide's definition of insider threat still cover this case?

options.text: Yes — insider threat covers harm by someone with legitimate access whether it is deliberate or accidental, and a misdirected or misconfigured disclosure is the accidental case named directly.
options.why: The guide's definition explicitly includes accidental harm — a misdirected file or a public bucket — alongside deliberate theft or sabotage.

options.text: No, since insider threat only applies when the person acted with deliberate malicious intent.
options.why: The guide's definition is explicit that accidental harm — including a public bucket — is covered alongside deliberate theft or sabotage.

options.text: No, because this is properly classified as an attack-surface issue rather than an insider one, when attack surface concerns the total set of reachable points on a system rather than harm caused by someone already holding legitimate access.
options.why: Attack surface concerns the total set of reachable points on a system, a different concept from harm caused by someone who already holds legitimate access.

options.text: No, since only actions taken by permanent employees, not contractors or partners, count as insider threat.
options.why: The guide's definition names employees, contractors, and partners alike as potential insiders, so employment type is not what excludes a case.

items.rationale: Insider threat is harm caused by someone who already holds legitimate access, whether deliberate — theft, sabotage — or accidental, such as a misdirected file, a public bucket, or a deleted database. Intent is not the qualifying condition; legitimate access to cause the harm is.

items.stem: A team reads a CVE identifier and assumes it already tells them how severe the flaw is. What does a CVE identifier actually name, and where does severity come from instead?

options.text: The identifier is only a name for the defect, assigned by a CVE Numbering Authority; severity comes from a separate CVSS score.
options.why: The guide is explicit that confusing a CVE identifier with a CVSS score is a direct, testable error — the identifier lets everyone refer to the same defect, nothing more.

options.text: The sequence number in the identifier itself encodes the CVSS score, so a higher number means a more severe flaw.
options.why: The sequence number is only an assignment order from the numbering authority and carries no severity information at all.

options.text: Severity comes from how large the affected package's attack surface is, not from any separate score, when attack surface describes total exposure independent of any one defect, while CVSS is the actual severity scoring system for a specific catalogued flaw.
options.why: Attack surface describes total exposure independent of any one defect; CVSS is the actual severity scoring system for a specific catalogued flaw.

options.text: Severity comes from how the flaw is classified in the risk-threat-vulnerability framework, not from a numeric score.
options.why: The risk framework combines likelihood and impact qualitatively; the numeric 0.0-10.0 severity for a specific CVE is CVSS, a distinct and separately maintained score.

items.rationale: A CVE identifier of the form CVE-YYYY-NNNN is a name for a publicly known defect, assigned by a CVE Numbering Authority; it carries no severity information. CVSS is the separate 0.0 to 10.0 scoring system that supplies severity, and databases such as the National Vulnerability Database enrich CVE records with those scores.

items.stem: A patch team has to choose between a CVE scored 9.8 in a package that is installed but never run and unreachable from any network, and one scored 6.5 in a package actively serving the internet-facing login. Which should be prioritised, and on what basis?

options.text: The 6.5 on the login service, because deployment and reachability — not the raw CVSS number alone — should drive patch priority.
options.why: The guide states directly that a 9.8 in software that is never run and unreachable may matter less than a 6.5 on an internet-facing service, since exposure is what turns a score into actual risk.

options.text: The 9.8, because CVSS base score alone determines patch order regardless of where the package is deployed.
options.why: The guide names this exact ranking as the trap: a CVSS base score describes the flaw in the abstract, not deployment context, which is what actually determines risk.

options.text: Neither should be prioritised over the other until a penetration test confirms both are exploitable, when reachability and deployment context are already known here and sufficient to prioritise without requiring an exploitation attempt first.
options.why: Reachability and deployment context are already known and sufficient to prioritise; a penetration test is not a prerequisite for an ordinary patch-priority decision.

options.text: The 9.8, because patching it also reduces the host's overall attack surface more than patching the 6.5 would.
options.why: Patching a named defect in software that keeps running does not reduce attack surface at all; that is a separate remediation, not a reason to rank this CVE higher.

items.rationale: Patch priority should follow severity, whether the affected component is actually deployed and reachable, and whether exploitation is observed in the wild — not the raw CVSS number in isolation. An unreachable, unused package's high score matters less than a lower score on a service actively exposed to attackers.

items.stem: A team hardens a freshly provisioned host once at build time and never revisits the configuration. Why does the guide treat hardening as something verified periodically rather than done once?

options.text: Because configuration drifts as software is installed and rules are added, so a baseline that was correct at build time can become permissive again over time.
options.why: The guide names configuration drift specifically as the reason a one-time hardening pass is insufficient, and periodic verification is what catches it.

options.text: Because CIS Benchmarks are updated so frequently that any host is out of date within days regardless of drift, when benchmark update cadence is not the reason periodic verification matters — ordinary operational drift on the host itself is.
options.why: Benchmark cadence is not the reason periodic verification matters; the guide points to configuration drift on the host itself, from ordinary operational changes.

options.text: Because vendors patch default installations weekly, making any earlier hardening pass obsolete.
options.why: Patching addresses named defects, a separate concern from whether unnecessary services, accounts, or ports have crept back in since the initial hardening pass.

options.text: Because attack surface only ever grows through newly disclosed CVEs, not through configuration changes.
options.why: Attack surface grows through configuration changes too — a newly installed package or re-enabled account — which is exactly the drift hardening verification is meant to catch.

items.rationale: Vendors ship for broad usability, and a hardening baseline applied once reflects the system's state at that moment only. As software is installed and rules are added over the system's life, configuration drifts away from that baseline, which is why hardening is verified periodically against a published standard rather than treated as a one-time task.

items.stem: A fresh Linux install ships with several services enabled and a permissive default account that most administrators never need. Why does this happen, and whose responsibility is it to fix?

options.text: Vendors ship for broad usability rather than for any one threat model, so tightening the defaults for a specific deployment is the operator's hardening task.
options.why: The guide states plainly that a default installation is by definition more permissive than a deployed system needs, because vendors optimise for general usability.

options.text: It happens because the vendor made an oversight, and the fix is to wait for a vendor patch that disables the defaults.
options.why: This is not a defect to be patched; it reflects a deliberate usability trade-off the vendor made, which the deploying organisation is expected to tighten itself.

options.text: It happens because the CVE program has not yet catalogued the default configuration as a weakness, when a permissive default is not a discrete catalogued defect at all, but a deliberate usability trade-off the operator is expected to tighten.
options.why: A permissive default is not a discrete catalogued defect; it is expected behaviour a deploying organisation tightens through hardening, not something a CVE would name.

options.text: It happens only on systems without SELinux or AppArmor installed, and enabling either removes the need for hardening.
options.why: Mandatory access control confines what a process may do; it does not remove unnecessary services or accounts, which is a separate hardening task.

items.rationale: Vendors ship for broad usability rather than for any particular organisation's threat model, so a default installation is necessarily more permissive than most deployments need. Hardening — removing unnecessary packages, closing ports, disabling unused accounts — is the deploying organisation's own task, not something a vendor patch resolves.

items.stem: A strong perimeter firewall protects a flat internal network. Once an attacker gets past that perimeter, what stops them from reaching every other host inside?

options.text: Nothing, on a flat network — segmentation is the control that limits lateral movement once inside, and the perimeter firewall alone does not provide it.
options.why: The guide states this exactly: a strong perimeter firewall around a flat internal network still leaves an attacker who gets inside free to move laterally, which segmentation is what addresses.

options.text: The same perimeter firewall, since its rule set is re-evaluated continuously against every internal connection too, when a perimeter firewall filters what crosses the boundary it sits on and does not by itself constrain traffic already moving between internal hosts.
options.why: A perimeter firewall filters what crosses the boundary it sits on; it does not by itself constrain traffic moving between hosts already inside a flat network.

options.text: Full disk encryption on each host, since an encrypted disk cannot be reached from elsewhere on the network.
options.why: Full disk encryption protects data if the physical device is lost; it has no bearing on whether a running, unlocked host is reachable over the network.

options.text: SSH hardening on the perimeter firewall's own management interface.
options.why: Hardening the firewall's own management access protects that one device; it does nothing to stop lateral movement between other hosts once an attacker is already inside.

items.rationale: A firewall decides what may cross the boundary it sits on; segmentation decides how many boundaries exist to cross at all. A strong perimeter firewall around a flat internal network still leaves an attacker who gets past it free to move laterally, which is the specific failure zero trust and segmentation both respond to.

items.stem: A stateful firewall permits an outbound connection from an internal host to a remote service. Does it need a separate inbound rule to allow that service's response traffic back in?

options.text: No — a stateful firewall tracks connection state and allows return traffic for a permitted outbound flow without a separate inbound rule.
options.why: Stateful filtering is precisely what lets return traffic for a permitted flow through automatically, which is why the rule set can stay default-deny elsewhere.

options.text: Yes, since every direction of traffic always needs its own explicit rule regardless of the firewall's design.
options.why: That describes a stateless design; a stateful firewall tracks the connection and admits the matching return traffic without a mirrored inbound rule.

options.text: No, but only because the internal host is also segmented into its own network zone.
options.why: Segmentation and stateful tracking are separate mechanisms; return traffic for a permitted flow is admitted by the stateful property itself, independent of zoning.

options.text: Yes, unless the connection uses TLS, in which case the encrypted channel bypasses the firewall's rules entirely, when stateful tracking already admits return traffic for a permitted flow regardless of whether that traffic happens to be encrypted under TLS.
options.why: TLS encrypts the payload but does not exempt the connection from firewall filtering, and stateful tracking already handles return traffic without needing this exception.

items.rationale: Rules are written default-deny — permit what is required, drop everything else — and a stateful firewall tracks connection state so return traffic for a permitted outbound flow is allowed automatically, without a separate inbound rule having to mirror it.

items.stem: A team wants a system that can actually drop malicious packets, not just alert on them. What placement decision does that requirement force, and what is the operational trade-off it carries?

options.text: The system must sit inline in the traffic path to be able to drop packets, and that placement means a false positive drops legitimate traffic too.
options.why: The guide is explicit that a prevention system must sit inline because dropping packets requires being on the path, and that inline placement is exactly what makes a false positive costly.

options.text: The system can stay on a passive tap or mirrored port and still block traffic once it detects it, when blocking traffic requires sitting inline on the path itself, which a passive tap or mirrored port position cannot provide however good the detection is.
options.why: A passively placed system, off the direct traffic path, cannot drop packets however good its detection is — blocking requires inline placement.

options.text: The placement decision only matters for host-based deployments, not for network-based ones.
options.why: The inline-versus-passive distinction applies to network deployments (NIPS versus NIDS) just as much as host-based ones, since either can be placed to observe or to intervene.

options.text: The system should instead be deployed as a vulnerability scanner, since scanners can already block traffic once a weakness is found.
options.why: A vulnerability scanner enumerates known weaknesses on a schedule; it has no role in blocking live traffic, which is what this requirement is about.

items.rationale: The difference between detection and prevention is placement and authority, not analytical power: a prevention system must sit inline, in the traffic path, because it has to be able to drop packets, while a detection system commonly sits passively and cannot. Inline placement is also why many deployments run detection-only first, since a false positive there drops legitimate traffic.

items.stem: An IDPS and a vulnerability scanner are compared as a pair. What is the separating axis between what each one answers?

options.text: Present tense versus latent state — the IDPS answers whether something is happening right now, while the scanner answers what could be exploited if someone tried.
options.why: The comparison names this exact axis: continuous observation of live activity versus a scheduled or pipeline-run check of configured state.

options.text: Cost — the IDPS is always cheaper to run than a vulnerability scanner.
options.why: Relative cost is not the property the comparison table tracks; it separates the two by what each examines and when it runs, not by price.

options.text: Both answer exactly the same question, and either one substitutes for the other in a mature security programme.
options.why: The guide states directly that neither substitutes for the other; one watches live activity continuously and the other checks configured state on a schedule.

options.text: Only the vulnerability scanner can be deployed on a host; the IDPS only ever runs on network infrastructure, when host-based deployment (HIDS/HIPS) is one of the IDPS's own two forms alongside the network-based one, not something reserved for a scanner.
options.why: IDPS deployment includes both network-based (NIDS/NIPS) and host-based (HIDS/HIPS) forms, so host deployment is not exclusive to the scanner.

items.rationale: An IDPS examines live traffic and host activity continuously, answering whether an attack is happening right now; a vulnerability scanner examines configured state on a schedule or in a build pipeline, answering what could be exploited if someone tried. Neither substitutes for the other, since one is initiated by the attacker's activity and the other by you.

items.stem: A question asks "why ship logs off the originating host to a central SIEM." Is that question testing accounting, or security logging and monitoring?

options.text: Security logging and monitoring — it asks about the operational pipeline that makes records survive and get seen, not about the AAA-triad property of recording actions.
options.why: The guide draws this line directly: accounting is the per-identity record itself, while shipping, clock synchronisation, retention and alerting are this topic's operational pipeline.

options.text: Accounting, since shipping logs off-host is just another way of describing the third A of AAA.
options.why: The guide states these are close enough to test as separate concepts: accounting is the recorded event itself, while log shipping and SIEM architecture belong to this topic instead.

options.text: Neither — shipping logs off-host is an availability concern addressed by redundancy, not by either topic.
options.why: Shipping logs protects the integrity and usefulness of the evidence, not availability of a service, and it is squarely part of this topic's operational pipeline.

options.text: Accounting, because a SIEM is defined as the tool that performs authentication decisions for every host it collects from, when a SIEM's role is collecting and correlating events across hosts, not making authentication decisions for any of the systems it monitors.
options.why: A SIEM collects and correlates events; it does not perform authentication decisions for the hosts it monitors, which is unrelated to what log shipping is for.

items.rationale: Accounting is the AAA-triad property — the per-identity record of what an authenticated subject did. Security logging and monitoring is the operational pipeline that makes such records survive and get seen: generation on every host, shipping off-box, clock synchronisation, retention, and alerting. A question about why logs are shipped to a SIEM tests this pipeline, not accounting itself.

items.stem: Events from a database server, a web server, and a firewall arrive at a central collector with unsynchronised clocks. What does that unsynchronised state prevent an investigator from doing?

options.text: Correlating the events into an accurate timeline, since matching activity across systems depends on their clocks agreeing.
options.why: The guide names clock synchronisation specifically so events from different systems can be correlated into a timeline; without it, ordering events across hosts becomes unreliable.

options.text: Reading any individual log entry at all, since unsynchronised clocks make log files unreadable, when unsynchronised clocks affect the reliability of ordering events across systems rather than the readability of any single host's own log file.
options.why: Unsynchronised clocks affect the reliability of cross-system ordering, not the readability of any single log file on its own.

options.text: Retaining the logs for the required period, since retention depends on clock accuracy.
options.why: Retention is a separate setting governing how long records are kept; it does not depend on whether clocks across hosts agree with each other.

options.text: Encrypting the logs in transit to the collector, since TLS requires synchronised clocks to function.
options.why: TLS certificate validation checks clock time against a certificate's validity window, but ordinary log shipping to a collector does not require synchronised clocks to encrypt successfully.

items.rationale: Clocks are synchronised across hosts specifically so events from different systems can be correlated into a single, accurate timeline. Without that synchronisation, an investigator cannot reliably determine the order in which activity occurred across the database, web, and firewall logs, even though each individual log remains readable.

items.stem: A study note attributes the six-step prepare-identify-contain-eradicate-recover-learn sequence to NIST SP 800-61. Is that attribution correct?

options.text: No — that six-step sequence is SANS's model, commonly abbreviated PICERL; no revision of NIST SP 800-61 has ever published it.
options.why: The guide corrects this exact misattribution: Rev. 2 used a four-phase lifecycle and Rev. 3 replaced that with the six CSF 2.0 Functions, neither of which is PICERL.

options.text: Yes, and it has appeared unchanged in every revision of NIST SP 800-61 since it was first published.
options.why: This misattribution is exactly what the guide flags as routinely made; the six-step sequence is SANS's PICERL, not a NIST SP 800-61 model at any revision.

options.text: Yes, because NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 renamed its four-phase lifecycle into these exact six steps in 2025.
options.why: Rev. 3 replaced the four-phase lifecycle with the six CSF 2.0 Functions — Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover — a different six-item list from PICERL, not a renaming of it.

options.text: No, because the six-step sequence actually comes from the CIA triad's own incident classification scheme, when the CIA triad classifies which security property an incident affects and is not the source of any response-process sequence.
options.why: The CIA triad classifies which security property an incident affects; it is not the source of any incident-response process sequence.

items.rationale: The six-step prepare, identify, contain, eradicate, recover, learn sequence — commonly abbreviated PICERL — is SANS's model. NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 used a distinct four-phase lifecycle, and Rev. 3 (April 2025) replaced that with the six CSF 2.0 Functions, a different six-item list built around cybersecurity risk management broadly rather than one incident's tactical handling.

items.stem: A responder finds an intrusion and immediately wipes and rebuilds the affected host before establishing how far the attacker spread. What did skipping ahead of containment cost, in PICERL terms?

options.text: It destroyed the evidence needed to establish scope, so it can no longer be confirmed whether the attacker is still present elsewhere.
options.why: Containment precedes eradication precisely because stopping the spread first preserves the investigation; wiping and rebuilding before scope is known destroys that evidence.

options.text: Nothing was lost, since eradication and containment achieve the same outcome regardless of order.
options.why: The guide states directly that acting out of sequence is the characteristic wrong answer, and order matters here because eradicating first destroys evidence containment would have preserved.

options.text: It skipped the preparation phase, which should have happened at this point in the sequence instead.
options.why: Preparation is the phase completed before anything happens — plans, contacts, tested backups — not a step that occurs mid-incident after identification.

options.text: It skipped the lessons-learned review, which always occurs immediately after identification rather than at the end, when the lessons-learned review is the final step after recovery, not one that belongs immediately following identification.
options.why: The lessons-learned review is the final step, occurring after recovery, not a step that belongs immediately after identification.

items.rationale: Containment isolates affected systems while investigation is still possible, and it precedes eradication for exactly that reason. Wiping and rebuilding before scope is established destroys the evidence needed to confirm whether the attacker is still present elsewhere, which is the concrete cost of acting out of order.

items.stem: An attacker gains physical console access to a locked-down server. Which of the installed system's software controls stop them from interrupting the boot loader to obtain a root shell?

options.text: None on the installed operating system itself — that requires boot-path controls such as a firmware password and a boot loader password, layered with physical access control.
options.why: The guide states directly that an attacker at the console operates below the level most software controls occupy, so boot-path and physical controls, not the installed OS, are what address this.

options.text: File permissions and authentication on the installed operating system stop this reliably.
options.why: The guide is explicit that authentication and file permissions on the installed system cannot prevent interrupting the boot loader, since the attacker acts before that system is even running.

options.text: SELinux or AppArmor in enforcing mode stops this, since mandatory access control confines every process on the host, when mandatory access control confines processes already running under the installed operating system and has no bearing on interrupting the boot sequence beforehand.
options.why: Mandatory access control confines processes running under the installed operating system; it has no bearing on interrupting the boot sequence before that system has started.

options.text: Full disk encryption alone stops this, since an encrypted volume cannot be booted into an alternate operating system.
options.why: Full disk encryption protects data confidentiality if the drive is removed; it does not by itself prevent interrupting the boot loader on the running hardware, which boot-path controls address.

items.rationale: An attacker at the console operates below the level most software controls occupy: interrupting the boot loader, booting from removable media, or simply removing the disk are none of them stopped by the installed system's authentication or file permissions. The layered answer combines physical access control with boot-path controls and full disk encryption, which is the piece that still holds once the hardware itself is in someone else's hands.

items.stem: A decommissioned drive is deleted through the operating system's normal file deletion before leaving the building. Is that sufficient for secure disposal?

options.text: No — media that leaves the building is wiped or destroyed rather than merely deleted, since ordinary deletion does not remove the underlying data.
options.why: The guide's practice for secure disposal is explicitly wiping or destruction, not ordinary file deletion, which typically leaves the underlying bytes recoverable.

options.text: Yes, since deleting a file through the operating system removes its data from the drive immediately, when ordinary deletion typically removes only the filesystem's pointer to the data and leaves the underlying bytes recoverable on the drive itself.
options.why: Ordinary deletion typically only removes the filesystem's reference to the data, not the underlying bytes, which is why the guide requires wiping or destruction instead.

options.text: Yes, as long as the drive was also protected by full disk encryption while it was in service.
options.why: Encryption while in service is a separate, valuable control, but the guide's stated disposal practice still calls for wiping or destroying the media, not relying on the earlier encryption state alone.

options.text: This question only applies to backup tapes, not to drives removed from a server.
options.why: Secure disposal applies to any media leaving the building, drives included, not only to tape backups specifically.

items.rationale: Ordinary file deletion typically removes only the filesystem's pointer to the data, leaving the underlying bytes recoverable. The guide's disposal practice is explicit: media that leaves the building is wiped or destroyed, not merely deleted, before it is decommissioned.

items.stem: An administrator sets `PasswordAuthentication no` in `sshd_config`, reloads the daemon, and users are still prompted for a password. `PermitRootLogin` is untouched at its default. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: `KbdInteractiveAuthentication` is still at its default `yes`, and on a PAM-backed system that path can still prompt for a password.
options.why: Turning off `PasswordAuthentication` alone is not sufficient, since the keyboard-interactive path defaults to `yes` and can still supply a password prompt through PAM.

options.text: The setting only takes effect after a full system reboot, not after a daemon reload.
options.why: Changes take effect when the daemon reloads its configuration; a reboot is not required, and the running session is unaffected only until that reload happens.

options.text: `PermitRootLogin` at its default `prohibit-password` is overriding `PasswordAuthentication` for all accounts, not just root, when `prohibit-password` only governs how root itself may authenticate and does not extend to overriding the setting for other named accounts.
options.why: `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password` only governs root's login method; it does not override the `PasswordAuthentication` setting for ordinary named accounts.

options.text: The public key was never generated with `ssh-keygen`, so the server falls back to a password prompt automatically.
options.why: Whether a client has a key pair does not change what the server's `sshd_config` permits; the server is still offering a password path because that directive is separately enabled.

items.rationale: Disabling `PasswordAuthentication` is not by itself sufficient to stop password entry: `KbdInteractiveAuthentication` defaults to `yes`, and on a PAM-backed system that path can still prompt for a password. A real baseline sets both to `no`.

items.stem: Right after a hardening change to `sshd_config`, a new connection attempt from a second terminal times out — it never even reaches a login prompt. The first, still-open session continues to work normally. Where should the administrator look first?

options.text: A firewall rule or security group blocking the connection, since nothing in `sshd_config` itself produces a timeout.
options.why: The guide's diagnostic order places a timeout outside `sshd_config` entirely: traffic never reaching the daemon points at a firewall rule or security group, not a server-configuration problem.

options.text: The `AuthorizedKeysFile` setting, since a wrong path there is the most common cause of a hung connection.
options.why: A wrong `AuthorizedKeysFile` produces a `Permission denied (publickey)` rejection once the daemon is reached, not a connection that times out before ever reaching it.

options.text: `StrictModes`, since a permissive `.ssh` directory always produces a silent timeout instead of an explicit rejection.
options.why: `StrictModes` causes the daemon to refuse to use a permissively-writable `authorized_keys` file, which is a rejection after reaching the daemon, not a pre-daemon timeout.

options.text: The `Port` directive, since changing it always causes new connections to time out until clients are updated.
options.why: A wrong port produces an immediate connection-refused or a client connecting to the wrong service, not a silent timeout, and moving the port is a documented, deliberate option rather than a fault by default.

items.rationale: The guide's diagnostic order treats a timeout as evidence that traffic is not reaching the daemon at all — a firewall rule or security group, not an `sshd_config` problem, since nothing in the server configuration itself produces that particular symptom. The still-open first session and the immediate rejection cases (refused, publickey denied) point to different, later-stage causes instead.

items.stem: A baseline sets `PermitRootLogin no`. A colleague argues this is redundant because `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password`, the default, already blocks root entirely. Are the two settings equivalent?

options.text: No — `prohibit-password` still permits root to log in with a key; only `no` disables root login outright.
options.why: The guide states this exact distinction: `prohibit-password` disables password and keyboard-interactive authentication for root while still permitting key-based root login, which `no` does not.

options.text: Yes, since both values block every method of root login identically.
options.why: This is the exact trap the guide names: `prohibit-password` is not the same as `no`, because key-based root login still succeeds under the default.

options.text: Yes, because `PasswordAuthentication no` elsewhere in the file already makes the `PermitRootLogin` value irrelevant.
options.why: `PasswordAuthentication` governs password login generally, but `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password` independently still allows root to authenticate by key regardless of that other setting.

options.text: No, but only because `prohibit-password` additionally requires MFA for any root login attempt.
options.why: Neither value has anything to do with MFA enrolment; the distinction is specifically about which authentication method root is still permitted to use.

items.rationale: `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password`, the OpenSSH default, disables password and keyboard-interactive authentication for root but still permits root to log in with a key. Only `PermitRootLogin no` disables root login outright, which is why a baseline that wants no direct root access at all sets it explicitly rather than relying on the default.

items.stem: Two directives for the same keyword appear in `sshd_config` — one in the main file, one in a drop-in file included earlier via `Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf` near the top. Which value does OpenSSH actually use, and which command reveals it without guessing?

options.text: The drop-in file's value wins, because unless a keyword documents otherwise the first obtained value is used — and `sshd -T` prints the effective configuration to confirm it.
options.why: `sshd_config` is first-obtained-value, the opposite of most configuration formats' last-wins behaviour, and `sshd -T` is the documented way to see which value actually took effect.

options.text: The main file's value wins, since directives placed later in a file always override ones read earlier.
options.why: This is last-wins reasoning, which is the opposite of `sshd_config`'s actual first-obtained-value behaviour — the earlier-included drop-in value wins instead.

options.text: Neither wins outright; `sshd` merges both values and applies whichever is more restrictive.
options.why: `sshd_config` does not merge conflicting scalar directives by restrictiveness; it takes the first value it obtains and ignores subsequent ones for that keyword.

options.text: The drop-in file's value wins, and `sshd -t` is what prints the effective merged configuration to confirm it, when `sshd -t` only validates syntax and reports errors before a reload, and it is `sshd -T` that actually prints the effective configuration.
options.why: `sshd -t` only validates syntax and reports errors before a reload; it is `sshd -T` that prints the effective configuration a drop-in file may be overriding.

items.rationale: `sshd_config` follows first-obtained-value semantics — the opposite of most formats — so a drop-in file included earlier in the main file wins over a directive written further down. `sshd -T` prints the effective configuration, which is the documented way to confirm which value is actually in force rather than guessing from file order alone.

items.stem: `getenforce` reports `Permissive` on a Red Hat host running a web service. A colleague reads this as "SELinux is protecting the service." Is that reading correct?

options.text: No — permissive mode logs what policy would have denied and permits it anyway, so the service is not actually confined.
options.why: The guide names this exact trap: `getenforce` distinguishes enabled from enforcing, and permissive mode is explicitly not protection despite still being active.

options.text: Yes, since `Permissive` means SELinux is active and confining every process on the host, with policy denials both logged and enforced as they occur.
options.why: This is precisely the misreading the guide corrects: `Permissive` means denials are logged but still allowed, which is not confinement.

options.text: Yes, because `Permissive` is simply AppArmor's name for what SELinux calls `Enforcing`.
options.why: `Permissive` is one of SELinux's own three modes alongside `enforcing` and `disabled`; it is not an AppArmor term at all.

options.text: This cannot be determined from `getenforce` alone; only `aa-status` reveals whether policy is actually being applied.
options.why: `getenforce` is exactly the command that reports SELinux's mode; `aa-status` reports AppArmor's state instead and would not apply to this Red Hat host's SELinux question.

items.rationale: SELinux being enabled and SELinux being enforcing are different claims, and `getenforce` is what distinguishes them. Permissive mode logs what policy would have denied and permits it anyway, so a service running under it is not actually confined despite SELinux being active.

items.stem: "SELinux and AppArmor" and "access control models" are compared as a pair. What separates them, given that both discuss mandatory access control?

options.text: Instance versus category — SELinux and AppArmor are specific Linux products implementing mandatory access control, while access control models is the taxonomy of discretionary, mandatory, and role-based schemes itself.
options.why: The comparison's separating axis is exactly this: one names concrete tools you install, configure and query, the other names the classification scheme those tools are examples within.

options.text: SELinux and AppArmor implement role-based access control specifically, while access control models covers only discretionary and mandatory.
options.why: SELinux and AppArmor implement the mandatory model, not the role-based one, and access control models as a taxonomy covers all three schemes including role-based.

options.text: SELinux and AppArmor are Linux-specific, while access control models only describes Windows and macOS systems, when access control models is an operating-system-agnostic taxonomy that is not scoped to any one platform's tooling.
options.why: Access control models is an operating-system-agnostic taxonomy, not one scoped to particular platforms other than Linux.

options.text: Only access control models is examinable by command; SELinux and AppArmor are conceptual only.
options.why: The reverse is true — SELinux and AppArmor are the command-bearing concept here, queried with `getenforce` and `aa-status`, while access control models is the conceptual taxonomy.

items.rationale: The separating axis is instance versus category: SELinux and AppArmor are specific products implementing one of the models, queried through commands like `getenforce` and `aa-status` and configured through `/etc/selinux/config` or AppArmor profiles, while access control models names the broader classification scheme — discretionary, mandatory, role-based — that those products are examples within.

items.stem: A team downloads a checksum file from the same page and the same server as the software it is meant to verify, runs `sha256sum` with `-c` against it, and gets `OK`. Does that establish the download is authentic?

options.text: No — a checksum from the same compromised source as the download proves only self-consistency; `gpg --verify` against a key obtained independently is what establishes origin.
options.why: The guide states directly that fetching the digest file from the same channel as the download means a matching digest proves only self-consistency, not authenticity.

options.text: Yes, since an `OK` result from `sha256sum -c` proves both integrity and origin, because the digest is cryptographically bound to the file it describes.
options.why: A checksum proves only that bytes match a value; it says nothing about who produced that value, which is exactly the trap the guide describes for a same-server digest.

options.text: Yes, as long as the digest file was downloaded over an HTTPS connection, since transport encryption authenticates whoever served the digest.
options.why: TLS protects the connection during transfer, but it does not establish that the source server itself was not the one compromised in the first place.

options.text: No, and the fix is to also run `md5sum` on the same file and compare the two results, since agreement between two algorithms would rule out tampering.
options.why: Running a second, weaker hash algorithm against the same self-consistent source adds no independent verification of origin; the missing step is a signature checked against an independently obtained key.

items.rationale: A checksum answers only whether the received bytes match a value; if that value came from the same compromised source as the download, a match proves self-consistency, not authenticity. `gpg --verify` checked against a signing key obtained through an independent, trusted channel is what actually establishes who released the bytes.

items.stem: `gpg --verify SHA256SUMS.asc SHA256SUMS` prints `Good signature` along with a warning that the signing key is not certified with a trusted signature. Should this be treated as a successful verification?

options.text: No — the signature matched a key, but the signer's identity is still unestablished until that key was obtained and validated through an independent, trusted channel.
options.why: The guide is explicit that a good-signature result alongside an uncertified-key warning means identity is unestablished; obtaining the key through an independent channel is the part that actually carries the security.

options.text: Yes, because `Good signature` is the only output that matters and the certification warning is purely informational.
options.why: The guide names ignoring exactly this warning as the trap: the signature matching a key you never validated does not establish the signer's identity.

options.text: No, because `gpg --verify` requires both a detached signature and a clearsigned document to be present simultaneously, when the detached form already takes exactly a signature file and a signed file together, which is the pair this command supplies correctly.
options.why: The detached form takes the signature file and the signed file together, or a clearsigned document alone — this command already supplies the correct detached pair; the actual gap is key certification, not file form.

options.text: Yes, but only if `sha256sum -c` was also run separately against the same SHA256SUMS file first.
options.why: Running a checksum check does not resolve the actual gap here, which is that the signing key itself was never validated through an independent, trusted channel.

items.rationale: A signature proves origin only relative to the key it was verified against. `Good signature` together with a warning that the key is not certified with a trusted signature means the cryptographic match succeeded but the signer's actual identity was never established — that establishment comes from obtaining the publisher's key through an independent, trusted channel, which is the step that most often gets skipped.

items.stem: A monthly scheduled scan reports zero findings on a host, and the scan ran unauthenticated, reading only what was exposed on the network. Is that a strong signal the host has no known weaknesses?

options.text: No — an unauthenticated scan only sees what is exposed on the network and systematically under-reports; a clean result is weak evidence because it never saw inside the host.
options.why: The guide states directly that a clean unauthenticated scan is weak evidence for exactly this reason, contrasted with an authenticated scan that reads installed package versions directly.

options.text: Yes, since an unauthenticated scan and an authenticated scan produce identical accuracy against a given host.
options.why: The guide contrasts the two explicitly: an authenticated scan logs in and reads package versions directly and is far more accurate than an unauthenticated one.

options.text: Yes, because a clean scan result also confirms no intrusion occurred on the host during the scan window.
options.why: A scan reports known weaknesses in current state; detecting an attack in progress is an intrusion detection system's job, which a vulnerability scan does not perform.

options.text: This cannot be assessed without also running a penetration test, since scanning and penetration testing produce equivalent results, when scanning enumerates and matches against a database while a penetration test attempts exploitation and chains findings, which are not equivalent activities.
options.why: Scanning enumerates and matches against a database, while a penetration test attempts exploitation and chains findings — the two are not equivalent, but the specific gap here is authentication depth, not the absence of a penetration test.

items.rationale: An authenticated scan logs in and reads installed package versions and configuration directly, making it far more accurate; an unauthenticated scan only sees what is exposed on the network and systematically under-reports. A clean unauthenticated result is therefore weak evidence of a host's actual state, since it never looked inside.

items.stem: A scanner finds a known weakness in a container's base image before it is ever deployed. Once that same image is running in production, what job does the scanner still not do that an IDPS does instead?

options.text: Detecting an attack actually happening against the running container in real time.
options.why: The comparison's axis is present tense versus latent state: the scanner lists known weaknesses in configured state, while noticing live activity as it happens is the IDPS's job.

options.text: Reporting the severity of the weakness it already found in the base image, which is already what a vulnerability scan reports through its matched database entries rather than the live-activity gap the question is asking about.
options.why: Severity reporting is exactly what a vulnerability scan already does through its matched database entries; the gap is live-activity detection, not severity scoring.

options.text: Verifying the checksum of the base image against the publisher's signed digest.
options.why: Checksum and signature verification is a separate supply-chain control performed at download time, not a gap between scanning and intrusion detection specifically.

options.text: Confining what the container process may do even if it is compromised.
options.why: Confining a compromised process is mandatory access control's job, which is a distinct layer from either scanning for known weaknesses or detecting live intrusions.

items.rationale: Scanning container images at build time catches a vulnerable base image before it ever runs, which is the same idea as host scanning moved earlier. Once deployed, a scan still only reports known weaknesses in current state on a schedule; noticing an attack actually happening against the running container is the IDPS's continuous, present-tense job instead.
